chunks.title: Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Severe bleeding is the leading preventable cause of death after injury. Act within seconds. Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with the heel of your hand, using any clean cloth as padding. Press hard enough that it is uncomfortable — light pressure does not stop arterial bleeding. Do not remove soaked dressings. Add more padding on top and keep pressing, because lifting the dressing tears away the clot that is forming. If the limb is bleeding uncontrollably and direct pressure fails, apply a tourniquet 5 to 7 cm above the wound, never over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops and the pulse below disappears. Write the time of application on the casualty's forehead or the tourniquet itself. Once a tourniquet is applied, do not loosen or remove it. Loosening releases accumulated toxins and restarts the bleeding. Lay the casualty down and keep them warm. Blood loss causes rapid heat loss, and cold blood clots poorly.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain first aid guidance (WHO/ICRC field manuals)

chunks.title: Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Infection usually appears 24 to 72 hours after injury. Watch for spreading redness, increasing rather than decreasing pain, swelling, heat, pus, or a foul smell. Red streaks running from the wound toward the body, fever, or chills indicate the infection is spreading through the lymphatic system. This is an emergency requiring antibiotics. Mark the edge of the redness with a pen and note the time. If the redness advances past the mark within a few hours, the infection is progressing rapidly. Any wound from an animal bite, a puncture from a dirty object, or a wound contaminated with soil carries tetanus risk and needs medical assessment.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain first aid guidance (WHO/ICRC field manuals)

chunks.title: Breathing and Cardiac Emergencies
chunks.text: For a child, use one or two hands and compress to about one third of the chest depth. For an infant, use two fingers in the centre of the chest just below the nipple line. Give 5 initial rescue breaths before starting compressions, because cardiac arrest in children is usually caused by a breathing problem rather than a heart problem. Use a compression to breath ratio of 30 to 2 if you are alone, or 15 to 2 with two trained rescuers. Do not tilt an infant's head as far back as an adult's. Over-extending the neck closes a small airway rather than opening it.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain resuscitation council guidance

chunks.title: Breathing and Cardiac Emergencies
chunks.text: Face: ask them to smile, and look for one side drooping. Arms: ask them to raise both arms, and see whether one drifts down. Speech: ask them to repeat a simple sentence, and listen for slurring or the wrong words. Time: if any of these are abnormal, note the time symptoms began and seek emergency care immediately. The time of onset determines which treatments are possible, so record it precisely. If they woke with symptoms, the relevant time is when they were last seen well. Give nothing to eat or drink. A stroke frequently impairs swallowing, and fluid entering the lungs causes pneumonia.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain resuscitation council guidance

chunks.title: Environmental Emergencies
chunks.text: Frostbite starts as numb, waxy, white or grey-yellow skin that feels hard or rubbery. Superficial frostbite still has soft tissue underneath; deep frostbite feels wooden throughout. Do not thaw a frozen limb if there is any chance it will refreeze. A refreeze cycle causes far worse tissue destruction than staying frozen during evacuation. Rewarm by immersion in water at 37 to 39 degrees Celsius — warm to the touch but not hot — for 20 to 30 minutes, until the tissue is red and pliable. Rewarming is intensely painful and pain relief will be needed. Do not rub the tissue, and do not use dry heat such as a fire or stove, because numb skin burns without the person feeling it. Separate affected fingers and toes with dry gauze, and do not walk on thawed feet.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain wilderness medicine guidance

chunks.title: Environmental Emergencies
chunks.text: Keep the person still and calm. Movement and a rising heart rate speed venom through the lymphatic system. Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint and keep it at or below heart level. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing before swelling begins. Mark the leading edge of the swelling with a pen and write the time, repeating every 15 minutes. This record helps clinicians judge envenomation. Do not cut the wound, do not attempt to suck out venom, do not apply ice, and do not use a tourniquet. All of these cause harm without removing venom. Photograph the snake only if it can be done from a safe distance. Do not attempt to catch or kill it — a second bite is a common and avoidable disaster. Antivenom is the only definitive treatment. Evacuate to a facility that stocks it.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain wilderness medicine guidance

chunks.title: Trauma and Sudden Collapse
chunks.text: Shock is the failure of circulation to deliver oxygen to tissue. It is caused by blood loss, severe burns, dehydration, severe infection, or anaphylaxis. Signs are pale, cold, clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, rapid shallow breathing, thirst, restlessness or anxiety, and later confusion and unconsciousness. A falling blood pressure is a late sign. Do not wait for it — treat on the basis of the skin, pulse, and mental state. Lay the person flat and raise the legs about 30 cm unless there is a leg fracture, spinal injury, or breathing difficulty. Keep them warm with insulation above and below, loosen tight clothing, and give nothing by mouth. Treat the cause: stop the bleeding, cool the burn, give adrenaline for anaphylaxis. Shock cannot be treated by positioning alone.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Trauma and Sudden Collapse
chunks.text: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, whole-body allergic reaction. Suspect it when a swollen face or tongue, a widespread rash, wheeze, throat tightness, or collapse follows a sting, food, or medication. Give adrenaline by auto-injector into the outer thigh immediately, through clothing if necessary. Adrenaline is the only treatment that reverses anaphylaxis; antihistamines are far too slow. Lay the person flat with legs raised. Do not stand them up or let them walk, because sudden upright posture during anaphylaxis can cause fatal cardiac arrest. A second dose may be given after five minutes if there is no improvement. Everyone who receives adrenaline must be observed in hospital, because symptoms can return several hours later.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Burns and Poisoning
chunks.text: For a chemical burn, brush off dry powder first, then flush with large volumes of running water for at least 20 minutes, and longer for alkalis, which keep penetrating. Flush away from the unaffected body so the runoff does not spread the chemical. Protect yourself — do not become a second casualty. Do not attempt to neutralise an acid with an alkali or the reverse. The reaction generates heat and worsens the injury. For an electrical burn, do not touch the person until the power is switched off at the source. High-voltage current can arc, so stay at least 18 metres away from downed power lines until the utility confirms isolation. Electrical injury causes deep tissue damage between an entry and exit wound that is far worse than the skin suggests, and can disturb heart rhythm for hours. All electrical injuries need medical assessment.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: Boiling is the most reliable method. Bring water to a rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes above 2000 metres altitude where the boiling point is lower. Filter cloudy water through cloth first and let it settle, because suspended particles shield microorganisms from both heat and chemical disinfection. Chemical disinfection with unscented household bleach uses two drops of 5 percent sodium hypochlorite per litre of clear water, doubled for cloudy water. Mix and wait 30 minutes; the water should smell faintly of chlorine. Chlorine and iodine do not reliably kill cryptosporidium. Where that is a risk, filter or boil instead. Solar disinfection works in clear plastic bottles laid on a reflective surface in full sun for six hours, or two days if overcast. Do not drink seawater, urine, or alcohol when short of water. All three consume more body water than they provide.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: Three of anything — three fires, three whistle blasts, three flashes — is the recognised distress signal. A signal mirror is visible for many kilometres. Aim by holding two fingers at arm's length toward the target and flashing the reflected light across them. A whistle carries far further than the voice and costs almost no energy. Use it in preference to shouting. Make ground signals large: at least 3 metres per stroke, in straight lines with high contrast against the background. V means assistance required, X means medical assistance required. Stay put once you are reported missing unless you must move for safety. A stationary group is far easier to find than a moving one.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: Get out and stay out. Do not return to a burning building for possessions. Crawl low under smoke, where the air is cooler and clearer. Most fire deaths are from smoke inhalation, not burns. Before opening a door, feel it with the back of your hand. If it is hot, use another route. If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop, and roll, covering your face with your hands. Close doors behind you as you leave. A closed door significantly slows a fire's spread and buys survivable time. Agree a meeting point outside so it is immediately clear whether anyone is unaccounted for.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance
